title: The user was right
text:
A woman in accounts reported that her computer was slow every afternoon. She wrote the time in the ticket: after three o'clock.

Three engineers looked at it. All three tested in the morning, found a healthy machine, and closed the ticket with the same three words: no fault found.

She raised it a fourth time. This time someone walked upstairs at 15:30 and watched her work. The machine took nine seconds to open a spreadsheet.

The backup software started at 15:00 and used almost everything the computer had. It had been set that way two years earlier by a person who no longer worked there.

The fix took four minutes. The backup now runs at seven in the evening.

The engineer's internal note is one line, and the team still quotes it. She told us when it happened in the first ticket, and we tested at a time she never complained about.

questions.q: Why did the first three engineers find nothing?
options: They tested in the morning, when the problem wasn't happening

questions.q: What was actually slowing the machine down?
options: A virus in a shared folder

questions.q: What does 'no fault found' mean here?
options: Testing showed nothing wrong with the machine
The fault was fixed on the spot

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
options: Test at the time the user says the problem happens
Ask users to write longer tickets

title: Eleven seconds under target
text:
For two years the support team was measured on one number: average handling time. The target was six minutes. They finished most months eleven seconds under it, and the manager put the figure on a slide every quarter.

The same twenty-odd people kept calling back. Nobody counted them, because nobody was asked to.

A new manager changed the measure to something harder to hit: the percentage of tickets that stayed closed for thirty days. Handling time disappeared from the wall.

Within a month the average call was ninety seconds longer. Engineers were asking a second question, checking the fix with the caller still on the line, and writing an internal note that the next person could actually use.

Repeat contacts fell by a third over the quarter. The knowledge base grew by 140 articles, most of them written by two people who had always wanted to and had never had the time.

The new manager is careful about what she says in public. Her line to the team was blunter. You will get whatever you measure, so measure the thing you actually want.

questions.q: What was the team originally measured on?
options: How long each call lasted on average

questions.q: What happened to call length after the change?
options: It rose by about ninety seconds
Problems were checked and documented properly before closing
Customers were charged for second calls

questions.q: What does the manager's line about measuring mean?
options: Targets shape behaviour, so the wrong target produces the wrong work
Only managers should see the numbers
Speed is the only useful measure
